To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the effect of transborder ethnic kin on conflict is curvilinear, and that it depends on whether the TEK group is excluded or included.
the effect of transborder ethnic kin groups on civil war onset is curvilinear, and that the effect is strongest when the TEK groups are excluded from their state.
(i) the size of the transborder ethnic kin group has a U-shaped effect on civil war onset and (ii) that the effect of the TEKS size is conditional on whether the TEK group controls its own state.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether transnational ethnic links are a blessing or a curse for the ethnic groups that have them, and how this depends on the political situation in the TEK's home state.
the question of why ethnic groups that are linked to large ethnic kin groups across state borders often remain surprisingly peaceful.
the question whether transnational ethnic kin can be a source of peace or a source of conflict.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the TEK group effect is contingent on the TEK group having its own state.
TEK groups can be a source of conflict when the challenger group has a large TEK group, but they can also dampen conflict when the incumbent group has a large and independent TEK group.
the presence of TEK groups is associated with higher levels of conflict, but that this effect is mitigated when the TEK group controls its own state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effect of TEK groups is not a linear function of their size, but a U-shaped one.
transborder ethnic kin can be an important factor that either increases or decreases the risk of civil war, depending on the circumstances under which they are located.
the size of the transborder kin group is a double-edged sword for ethnic challengers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effect of TEK groups on conflict onset is not uniform.
conflict onset is not only driven by the dyadic relationship between the two groups in the primary dyad but is also shaped by the dyadic relationships in the secondary dyad.
the conflict dampening effect of transborder ethnic kin is contingent on the TEK groups being politically relevant in the state of their residence.
